title: Fungal Keratitis: Diagnosis, Management, and Recent Advances
study_design: Review of the diagnosis, management, and recent advances in fungal keratitis.
clinical_background: Fungal keratitis is a major cause of microbial corneal infection that can lead to blindness, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Fungi rarely invade an intact cornea, but trauma, especially involving vegetable matter, immunosuppression, topical steroid use, and ocular surface disease can increase susceptibility. More than a million cases are estimated to occur each year; the risk of perforation is about 10%, and more than half of affected patients lose vision and live with monocular blindness. Diagnosis can be difficult to confirm in the laboratory, while the availability and effectiveness of antifungal treatments pose additional challenges. Prolonged, intensive topical treatment may be insufficient.
interpretation: Fungal keratitis can threaten vision, and prolonged topical antifungal treatment may be insufficient. Antifungal medication remains the principal treatment, while therapeutic keratoplasty may be necessary when infection progresses or complications develop. Intrastromal injection may sustain therapeutic drug levels in the cornea, and intracameral injection may help in severe, treatment-resistant disease with deep stromal infiltration. PACK-CXL has been proposed as an independent or adjunctive treatment, but the clinical evidence is mixed and its protocol requires further refinement.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: In MUTT I, topical natamycin produced significantly better visual outcomes and was associated with a lower risk of complications than topical voriconazole, particularly for Fusarium infection. MUTT II found that adding oral voriconazole exposed patients to systemic side effects without improving the final outcome, although other studies claimed beneficial effects from oral voriconazole. Intrastromal studies also differ: Solaiman et al reported faster resolution and a higher healing rate with adjunctive voriconazole, whereas Narayana et al found no benefit when it was added to primary treatment of filamentous fungal ulcers. Studies of intracameral antifungals often reported favorable responses, but the randomized trial by Sharma et al found no difference in healing time or final visual acuity compared with topical treatment and reported more cataracts. PACK-CXL studies likewise reported both improved healing or fewer complications and no added benefit over antimicrobial treatment.
clinical_implications: Clinical appearance can suggest fungal keratitis, but laboratory testing is needed to confirm the diagnosis and identify the organism; concurrent infection is also possible.
A poor response to antifungal medication or progressive deep infection may make targeted drug delivery or surgery relevant, although findings for these approaches are not uniformly favorable.
Toxicity from prolonged topical antifungal treatment can resemble persistent infection.
PACK-CXL may be useful in some fungal ulcers, particularly moderate or superficial disease, but its benefit as an adjunct is uncertain across the cited studies.
practice_implications: Obtain microbiological samples at presentation, before medication begins, and start antifungal therapy after clinical suspicion is confirmed by a smear or positive culture.

Use topical antifungal medication as the main medical treatment. The article identifies natamycin 5% as first-line therapy: administer it hourly until infiltration begins to resolve, then every 2 hours, and continue it for 2 weeks after infection resolution.

Add topical broad-spectrum antibiotics to guard against additional bacterial infection. Cycloplegic drops may be used for pain and associated iridocyclitis, and anti-glaucoma medication should be added if intraocular pressure is elevated.
Avoid topical steroids during active fungal keratitis because they reduce the efficacy of concurrent antifungal medication and worsen disease when used alone.

Consider systemic antifungals for large ulcers extending to the limbus, severe deep keratitis, associated scleritis or endophthalmitis, or prophylaxis after penetrating keratoplasty for fungal keratitis. The article states that systemic treatment must continue for 6–8 weeks.
Assess ulcer size, stromal infiltration depth and hypopyon when judging treatment response. If these findings persist or worsen, modify medical treatment and consider surgery.
If topical-treatment toxicity is suspected, especially after 6 weeks, stop the medication and monitor carefully to exclude ongoing infection.
Consider therapeutic keratoplasty when an ulcer progresses despite appropriate medical treatment or perforation is impending or measures >2 mm.

After therapeutic keratoplasty, continue antifungal treatment and monitor for recurrence. The article specifies at least 2 weeks of topical and systemic treatment when excision margins are infection-free, or at least 6–8 weeks when margins are infected or graft infection is clinically detected. Avoid postoperative topical corticosteroids unless infection is clinically well controlled.
Intracameral antifungal injection may be effective for severe fungal keratitis with deep stromal infiltration that has not responded to treatment.
Avoid CXL in active herpetic keratitis or in patients with a history of recurrent herpetic keratitis.
open_questions: Which UV fluence, irradiation duration and riboflavin concentration will optimize PACK-CXL and achieve 100% microbial killing?
The effects of Cyclosporin A on fungal growth are not well studied.
future_directions: Refine PACK-CXL protocols by investigating UV fluence, exposure time and riboflavin concentration.
Develop treatment approaches that act more rapidly and address antifungal resistance.
Investigate whether AI-assisted monitoring of progression and treatment response can support individualized care in the future.

tables.summary: The studies report variable outcomes with intrastromal antifungals. Some found faster healing or high success rates, whereas the Narayana et al trial found no benefit when intrastromal voriconazole was added to topical natamycin for primary treatment of filamentous ulcers. Reported complications include pain, bleeding, increased hypopyon, glaucoma and perforation.

tables.summary: Reports of intracameral treatment describe resolution in some deep infections, but comparative findings are mixed. The Sharma et al randomized trial found no improvement in success, healing time or final visual acuity and reported more cataracts; Nasrin et al found no significant success-rate difference from oral ketoconazole.

tables.summary: The PACK-CXL studies report contrasting findings: some describe healing or improvement, particularly in superficial disease, while others found no added benefit over antimicrobial treatment. The Prajna et el trial also raised the possibility of reduced visual acuity with adjunctive CXL.

main_conclusion: The authors recommend beginning antifungal treatment after clinical suspicion is confirmed by a smear or positive culture. Intrastromal injection may sustain therapeutic corneal drug exposure, intracameral injection may help severe deep infections that resist treatment, and CXL is proposed as a possible stand-alone or adjunctive treatment.
narrative_summary:
This review examines the diagnosis and management of fungal keratitis and summarizes published studies of intrastromal injection, intracameral injection and corneal collagen cross-linking. The authors emphasize that clinical appearances can suggest infection, but a smear or positive culture should confirm the diagnosis before antifungal treatment begins. Microbiological sampling is advised at presentation, before medication; culture also permits organism identification and susceptibility testing. Topical antifungals remain central to treatment. Natamycin 5% is presented as first-line therapy, while systemic treatment and targeted injections have roles in selected presentations. Topical steroids should be avoided during active fungal keratitis. Progressive ulcers despite appropriate medical treatment, or impending or actual perforation >2 mm, are indications given for therapeutic keratoplasty.

Findings from the cited injection studies are mixed. Some intrastromal studies report faster healing, whereas Narayana et al found no benefit from adding intrastromal voriconazole to topical natamycin as primary treatment for filamentous ulcers. Intracameral delivery may help severe, deep, nonresponding infection, but a randomized trial found no improvement in healing time or final visual acuity and reported more cataracts. PACK-CXL studies likewise include favorable reports and trials finding no added benefit. The authors propose CXL as a possible independent or adjunctive therapy, while noting that UV fluence, irradiation time and riboflavin concentration still require optimization.

secondary_results: The review describes culture as the most sensitive method for isolating fungal elements and notes that culture also permits organism identification, assessment of mixed infection, and in vitro susceptibility testing.
A lateral-flow device for Aspergillus identification in corneal scrapings and swabs was reported to have high diagnostic accuracy; no numerical accuracy measure is supplied.

IVCM can show fungal structures in vivo but cannot differentiate filamentous fungal types; repeat imaging of the same area is difficult, and resolution is limited for smaller organisms in mixed infections.

PCR may yield positive results after a few hours, whereas culture may require 2–14 days; the review notes PCR's cost, lack of susceptibility testing, difficulty assessing treatment efficacy, and possible contamination-related false positives.

In vitro rose Bengal PDAT activity was reported against Fusarium Solani, Aspergillus fumigatus, Candida albicans, and other fungi; the review also reports no resistance in the cited clinical experience.

CXL at 30 mW/cm2 for 3 min had an effect on corneal biomechanical stability equivalent to standard treatment in cited studies. Across 45–90 mW/cm2, the review reports no statistically significant biomechanical-stability difference from corresponding lower-intensity treatment.
Tabibian et al found that accelerated PACK-CXL at 9 mW/cm2 for 10 min reduced infiltration and increased healing.
Awad et al reported better clinical, microbiological, and pathological outcomes in rabbit eyes at higher UVA fluences of up to 15 J/cm2; these are animal findings, not patient outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Fungal keratitis is a major cause of microbial keratitis and can result in corneal blindness. Diagnosis is complicated by difficulty obtaining laboratory confirmation, while treatment is limited by the availability and effectiveness of antifungal drugs; prolonged, intensive topical treatment may be insufficient. Antifungal therapy is the principal treatment and is recommended after clinical suspicion has been confirmed by a smear or positive culture. Topical treatment is central, although systemic, intrastromal, and intracameral administration are possible. Therapeutic keratoplasty is the principal accepted surgical procedure and has a good success rate. Intrastromal delivery may maintain therapeutic concentrations within the cornea. Intracameral delivery may help severe, treatment-resistant disease with deep stromal involvement. Collagen cross-linking has been proposed either alone or alongside antifungal medication, but its UV fluence, irradiation duration, and riboflavin concentration require further refinement to achieve 100% microbial killing.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Infectious corneal ulcers, also termed microbial keratitis, are a leading cause of visual loss, particularly in developing countries. Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites can cause them. Microbial proliferation and inflammation destroy corneal tissue, reduce transparency, and impair vision. Fungi rarely invade an intact cornea but can become pathogenic with immunosuppression, trauma—especially trauma involving vegetable matter—topical steroid exposure, or ocular surface disease. Fungal keratitis, also called mycotic keratitis (MK), is an important cause of microbial keratitis and possible corneal blindness, particularly in tropical and subtropical countries. More than a million cases are estimated to be diagnosed annually; perforation risk is about 10%, and more than half of affected patients lose vision and live with monocular blindness. Laboratory identification is difficult, and antifungal availability and efficacy pose treatment problems. Intensive, prolonged topical therapy may be inadequate, warranting consideration of systemic, intrastromal, or intracameral delivery. New treatments are also needed to produce faster responses and address drug resistance.

document_sections.heading: Etiological Organisms
document_sections.content: Corneal fungal pathogens include filamentous fungi or molds, such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, Paecilomyces, Curvularia, and other phaeohyphomycetes; yeast and yeast-like fungi, such as Candida, Cryptococcus, and Geotrichum; and dimorphic fungi, such as Coccidioides and Histoplasma.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Fungal infection is described as the second most common cause of infectious keratitis after bacterial infection and as more severe and destructive. Its prolonged course carries substantial risks of complications and perforation, so therapeutic keratoplasty is frequently necessary. Incidence depends strongly on geography, humidity, and other local risk factors, even within one country. Most reports place fungal disease at 17% to 36% of corneal infections; reported proportions are 5–20% in the United States and more than 50% in developing countries. A recent Egyptian delta study reported fungal infection in as many as two-thirds of microbial keratitis cases, with culture-confirmed mixed infection in 20% of those fungal cases. Any age can be affected, but disease is more frequent in middle-aged people and in males. It is reported to be more endemic in winter because of humidity. Filamentous fungi predominate over yeast and yeast-like fungi; Aspergillus and Fusarium are the filamentous organisms most often observed, and Candida is the commonest yeast.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Features
document_sections.content: Assessment of suspected disease should establish onset and course, which are usually insidious and gradual, and inquire about trauma, contact lenses, systemic illness, and medication use. Symptoms include blurred vision, irritation, redness, photophobia, tearing, and discharge. Pain is usually less pronounced than in bacterial or Acanthamoeba keratitis and does not track the clinical findings. Findings include circumcorneal ciliary hyperemia, corneal infiltration and edema, diminished corneal luster, and typically feathery ulcer margins. Grey or yellow stromal infiltration commonly extends past the ulcer edge. A grey infiltrative ring can appear as raised, fluffy lesions with dirty yellow or brown pigmentation; dense endothelial-level infiltration may form plaques. Multifocal satellite microabscesses occur in more than 10% of cases, and thick hypopyon occurs in more than half. Appearance varies with the causative species. Serrated or feathery margins, raised borders, satellites, and infiltrate color can assist clinical distinction from bacterial keratitis. Candida and other yeast-associated ulcers may have a collar-button configuration: typically a small ulcer with expanding stromal infiltration. Although they resemble bacterial ulcers, they progress more slowly, have more discrete stromal infiltration, and do not respond to topical antibiotics. The illustrated examples include early and advanced ulcers, satellite lesions, hypopyon, and subsequent corneal opacity and vascularization.

document_sections.heading: Laboratory Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Clinical findings support an initial impression, but confirmation and organism identification require additional testing, including microbiology; concurrent infection should be considered. Microbiological specimens should be obtained at presentation, before medication begins. Corneal scraping provides material for microscopy and culture and also removes fungal burden and surface tissue, potentially improving drug penetration. A spatula or surgical blade is preferred over swabs or sponge-like materials, and sampling along the ulcer base and edge is advised. Endothelial plaques or deep keratitis may call for an anterior chamber tap; corneal biopsy is another option. When indicated, contact lenses and their solutions, previously used topical drugs, and eye cosmetics should also be cultured. A lateral-flow device assessed on corneal scrapings and swabs from suspected cases showed high diagnostic accuracy for Aspergillus species.

document_sections.heading: Direct Microscope
document_sections.content: Direct examination of corneal smears is an important early laboratory step. Options include Gram stain, Giemsa stain, and a potassium hydroxide (KOH) wet preparation. A recent report also described trypan blue staining for fungal-ulcer diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: KOH Wet Mount Preparation
document_sections.content: KOH at 10–20% dissolves human tissue while leaving alkali-resistant structures visible, permitting direct microscopic identification of fungi. This inexpensive, simple test has reported sensitivity ranging from 72% to 91%. An illustrated corneal scraping examined at X10 shows fungal filaments.

document_sections.heading: Gram and Giemsa Stains
document_sections.content: Gram and Giemsa stains are commonly used to detect microorganisms in clinical material. Gram staining can reveal fungal hyphae and stain yeasts; Giemsa stains many fungi blue, particularly yeasts and dimorphic fungi. Reported sensitivity for these stains ranges from 27% to 90%.

document_sections.heading: Trypan Blue Stain
document_sections.content: Trypan blue is used in ophthalmic procedures to stain the anterior lens capsule during cataract surgery, the Descemet membrane during endothelial keratoplasty, and epiretinal membranes during retinal procedures. More recently, staining of fungal filaments with trypan blue was reported to improve visualization, diagnosis, and photographic documentation. It is usually combined with KOH and applied after the preparation has dried on a glass slide.

document_sections.heading: Other Stains Used
document_sections.content: Lactophenol cotton blue, Grocott’s methenamine-silver stain, and Calcofluor white may also aid diagnosis, with reported sensitivity of 70% to 90%.

document_sections.heading: Fungal Culture
document_sections.content: Culture is considered the most sensitive approach to isolating fungi in suspected fungal keratitis. Besides identifying the pathogen, it helps detect mixed infection and assess in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility. Because no single medium detects all fungal infections, both selective and nonselective media should be used. Nonselective media can include blood agar; selective testing should include Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) supplemented with Gentamycin 50 µg/mL. Cycloheximide should not be included in SDA because it inhibits saprophytic fungi. Definitive diagnosis can be established when fungal elements are visible in a corneal smear; when a single medium grows fungus and the smear also contains fungus; when two or more media grow fungus despite a negative smear; or when a single solid medium shows confluent fungal growth at the inoculation site. Among positive cultures, fungal growth appears in more than 80% after 3 days and more than 95% after 7 days. Microbiologists should wait at least 7–14 days before declaring a fungal culture negative. Brain heart infusion can serve as a transport medium but is not routinely used. Yeasts and filamentous fungi readily grow on blood agar and SDA at room temperature. Placing agar in plastic bags can increase humidity and favor growth, which can be inspected visually or with a dissecting microscope.

document_sections.heading: Keratectomy and Biopsy
document_sections.content: Corneal biopsy obtained by diagnostic keratectomy provides greater diagnostic yield than scraping and may be considered when smears and cultures are negative. A 2–3 mm sterile disposable trephine is used for partial-thickness excision encompassing clear and infected cornea, followed by blade dissection of the base; the visual axis should be avoided. The procedure is generally performed with topical anesthesia under an operating microscope or slit lamp. Excised tissue undergoes microbiological and histopathological examination; a corneal button removed during therapeutic keratoplasty can also be examined. Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) are the histopathological stains most commonly used to identify fungal hyphae and inflammation.

document_sections.heading: Confocal Microscopy
document_sections.content: In vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) supplies real-time, high-resolution optical sections of the cornea’s microstructure, including stromal fibers, cells, and other intratissue material. It can noninvasively identify filamentous hyphae, yeasts, and in vivo hyphal density, potentially even early in disease. Available microscope types are tandem scanning, slit scanning, and laser scanning. Limitations include inability to distinguish filamentous fungal species, poor reproducibility when revisiting the same area, and inadequate resolution for smaller organisms in mixed infections.

document_sections.heading: Polymerase Chain Reaction
document_sections.content: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is described as a rapid, sensitive diagnostic method: positive findings can be available within a few hours, whereas culture may require 2–14 days. Most publications report sensitivity of more than 90%. Its limitations are cost, inability to test drug susceptibility, difficulty assessing treatment efficacy, and contamination-related false positives. Culture with susceptibility testing therefore remains the most specific diagnostic approach.

document_sections.heading: Artificial Intelligence and Its Role in Fungal Keratitis
document_sections.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) may contribute to diagnosis, monitoring, and management of infectious keratitis. Developed algorithms seek to distinguish fungal infection from other infectious causes and categorize fungal species using slit-lamp photographs, confocal images, and clinical information. Compared with experienced observers, the model developed by Saini et al had 100% specificity for fungal infection and 77% specificity for bacterial infection. AI may also monitor progression and treatment response and could eventually support individualized therapy.

document_sections.heading: Misdiagnosis of Fungal Keratitis
document_sections.content: Misdiagnosis can result from limited clinician experience distinguishing microbial keratitis, shortages of diagnostic equipment and trained staff, infrequent routine scraping for culture, and lack of access to confocal microscopy. Consequently, hypopyon ulcers are often presumed bacterial and treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics; referral may follow only after treatment failure, ulcer progression, and additional complications. Dahlgren et al found fungal keratitis particularly difficult to diagnose, reporting sensitivity of 38% and specificity of 45%. Clinical assessment alone is unreliable even for corneal specialists: Dalmon et al reported that they distinguished fungal from bacterial cases clinically in approximately two-thirds of cases. Pythium keratitis is another difficult diagnostic mimic: many cases were initially considered suspected or unidentified fungal infections because clinical and microscopic appearances resemble fungal keratitis. Its post-culture diagnostic technique is difficult and not routinely used.

document_sections.heading: Management
document_sections.content: Treatment is principally medical; progressive resistant disease or complications may require surgery. Sharma et al proposed a topical, systemic, and targeted therapy (TST) protocol with an overall success rate approaching 80%. Corneal collagen cross-linking has recently emerged as another surgical approach for active disease. A management algorithm for different presentations is illustrated.

document_sections.heading: Medical Therapy
document_sections.content: Antifungal drugs are the main treatment. Starting them after confirmation of clinical suspicion by smear or positive culture is recommended. Topical administration is foundational, while systemic, intrastromal, or intracameral routes may also be used. Topical broad-spectrum antibiotics should be added to prevent superimposed bacterial infection. Cycloplegic drops may lessen pain and accompanying iridocyclitis; anti-glaucoma drugs should be added if intraocular pressure is elevated. Topical steroids should be avoided: they reduce antifungal effectiveness when coadministered and worsen disease when given alone.

document_sections.heading: Topical Antifungal Agents
document_sections.content: Natamycin 5% is considered first-line treatment and was the first approved antifungal medication. It should initially be administered hourly until partial resolution of infiltration indicates improvement, then every two hours, and continued for 2 weeks after infection resolves. Voriconazole, an azole derived from fluconazole, has demonstrated broad activity against filamentous fungi and yeasts. Topical voriconazole 1% is not commercially available but can be pharmacy-prepared. Its minimal inhibitory concentration is 0.5 μg/mL, lower than that of other imidazoles. It is a possible alternative to natamycin for resistant disease, alone or in combination. Topical amphotericin B 0.15% can be prepared when natamycin 5% fails and is also considered first-line for Candida keratitis; it is ineffective against Fusarium infection. Econazole 1% has been found as effective as natamycin 5% for filamentous disease. Fungistatic fluconazole 2% is usually combined with another antifungal, such as amphotericin B, for Candida or Aspergillus keratitis. Topical clotrimazole 1% is also available. The synthetic triazole Posaconazole, an analog of itraconazole, has been reported in multiple studies to act broadly against pathogenic fungi and may be used when disease resists natamycin and voriconazole. Echinocandins cause fungal cell lysis by inhibiting (1,3)-D-glucan synthesis. Caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin are commercially available echinocandins approved by the FDA for invasive systemic fungal infections; reports describe efficacy in refractory fungal keratitis. Mycotic ulcer treatment trial I (MUTT I) found that topical natamycin yielded significantly better visual-acuity outcomes and fewer complications than topical voriconazole, particularly with Fusarium. The authors suggest that, in non-Fusarium disease, voriconazole may produce comparable or better results, especially without an epithelial defect, because its smaller molecule penetrates better. Synergistic combinations mentioned are amphotericin B with flucytosine for Candida and natamycin with ketoconazole for filamentous infection. Because topical antifungal responses develop slowly over weeks, treatment generally lasts longer than for bacterial keratitis; duration varies with response and ranges between 4 to 6 weeks. An unchanged or worsening ulcer size, stromal-infiltration depth, or hypopyon indicates poor response and may prompt modification of medication and initiation of surgery. Susceptibility testing is difficult to obtain, and in vitro responses correlate poorly with in vivo responses, possibly contributing to treatment failure. Prolonged topical treatment can injure the ocular surface and mimic persistent fungal inflammation. When toxicity is suspected, especially after 6 weeks, medication should be stopped with careful follow-up to exclude ongoing infection. Reduced cellular infiltration, disappearance of satellites, and less pain support clinical improvement.

document_sections.heading: Systemic Antifungal Agents
document_sections.content: Oral or parenteral treatment may be indicated for large ulcers approaching the limbus, severe deep keratitis, or associated scleritis or endophthalmitis. It is also indicated prophylactically when penetrating keratoplasty is performed for fungal keratitis. Systemic treatment must continue for 6–8 weeks. Mycotic ulcer treatment trial II (MUTT II) found that adding oral voriconazole to topical treatment for filamentous fungal ulcers caused systemic adverse effects without improving the final outcome. Other studies, however, have claimed benefit from oral voriconazole alone or with topical antifungals.

document_sections.heading: Systemic Anti-Fungal Agents Include
document_sections.content: Oral voriconazole 200 mg twice daily penetrates ocular tissues well and can achieve the minimal inhibitory concentration with sustained drug levels. Oral ketoconazole is listed at 600 mg/day, with liver-function monitoring every 2 weeks after its use. Other listed options are oral itraconazole 200 mg/day, oral fluconazole 200 mg/day, and intravenous miconazole.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Therapy
document_sections.content: Therapeutic keratoplasty is the principal accepted operation for fungal keratitis. Emerging approaches include Rose Bengal Photodynamic therapy and Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking.

document_sections.heading: Therapeutic Keratoplasty (TKP)
document_sections.content: An ulcer may advance despite appropriate medication, perforate, and spread to the limbus, sclera, or uveal tract; delayed diagnosis or inappropriate treatment can increase complications. Therapeutic keratoplasty may then be needed to control infection, prevent more serious complications, and preserve globe anatomy. Indications are progression despite proper medical therapy and impending or actual perforation >2 mm. Trephination should retain a 1–1.5 mm zone of clinically unaffected clear cornea, without residual fungal infection in the peripheral cornea, to reduce recurrence. Interrupted sutures with slightly longer bites help avoid cheese-wiring of the recipient edge. Anterior chamber irrigation removes residual exudate or organisms; avoiding lens contact helps prevent posterior spread. Intracameral antifungal injection should be performed at completion, with intravitreal injection as well if endophthalmitis is suspected. Infection recurs in 6–16% of grafts after TKP. Recurrence risks include perforation, hypopyon, lens infection, infection reaching the limbus, and prolonged topical steroid use before transplantation. Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) can substitute for penetrating keratoplasty with less allograft rejection, less intraocular spread, and reduced need for postoperative steroids. Studies of big-bubble DALK report a safe approach with high success, elimination of central optical-zone infection, improved physiological graft survival, and infection recurrence of 7.5%. DALK cannot be performed if infection reaches the endothelium or perforation is present. The removed corneal button and other excised tissue must be examined microbiologically and pathologically. Culture and susceptibility testing can identify an unknown pathogen and active antimicrobials. Histopathology reveals fungal elements in 75% of patients. Stromal hyphae usually lie parallel to the corneal surface; perpendicular orientation is generally seen with steroid exposure or severe infection by virulent organisms. Postoperative antifungals primarily aim to prevent recurrence. Topical and systemic drugs might continue for at least 2 weeks when excision margins are histopathologically free of infection, alongside careful surveillance. If margins contain infection or graft infection becomes clinically apparent, both routes should continue for at least 6–8 weeks. Eradication is the principal surgical objective, while preventing graft rejection is also crucial. Topical corticosteroids should be avoided after surgery unless infection is clinically well controlled. Cyclosporin A may replace corticosteroids, although its effect on fungal growth has not been adequately studied.

document_sections.heading: New Modalities in the Treatment of Fungal Keratitis
document_sections.content: The approaches discussed are intrastromal and intracameral antifungal delivery, Rose Bengal Photo-Dynamic Antimicrobial Therapy (PDAT), and Photo-Activated Chromophore for Keratitis-Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking (PACK-CXL).

document_sections.heading: Intrastromal Therapy
document_sections.content: Intrastromal voriconazole or amphotericin B may maintain corneal drug concentrations and prevent levels from falling below therapeutic concentrations. Targeted delivery can also reach deeply infected stroma. The accompanying table summarizes studies of intrastromal antifungal injections. Most cited studies used amphotericin B 3–5 µg in 0.1 mL or voriconazole 50 μg/0.1 mL. Aydin et al combined Voriconazole 0.05 mg/0.1 mL + amphotericin B 0.01 mg/0.1 mL and reported 87.5% success; injections were repeated up to 18 times with nearly no complications. Saluja et al compared intrastromal voriconazole 50 ug/0.1 mL, amphotericin B 5 μg/0.1 mL, and natamycin 10 μg/0.1 mL, reporting 93.3% overall success. Voriconazole performed best; natamycin and amphotericin B produced similar visual outcomes, but natamycin healed faster. Most studies used one, two, or three injections. In an operating room under aseptic conditions, topical anesthesia with or without peribulbar anesthesia is used. Prepared drug is loaded into a disposable 1 mL insulin syringe fitted with a 30-gauge needle. Under microscopy, the bevel-down needle enters unaffected clear cornea obliquely to mid-stromal depth; up to 5 divided doses create a drug barrier around the ulcer until corneal hydration occurs. Three randomized control trials assessed intrastromal voriconazole 50 μg/0.1 mL. Solaiman et al reported faster healing and infiltration resolution in deep or resistant disease. Narayana et al found no benefit when it was added as primary treatment for filamentous fungal keratitis and reported increased hypopyon, glaucoma and perforation risks, decreased healing times, greater scarring, intrastromal bleeding, and postoperative pain.

Findings differ across studies: some describe improved healing with adjunctive injections, whereas others find no added benefit or report complications.

document_sections.heading: Intracameral Therapy
document_sections.content: Intracameral antifungal injection may help severe fungal keratitis with deep stromal infiltration that has not responded to treatment by delivering high drug levels to the anterior chamber. It should be performed in an operating room under strict asepsis. Anterior chamber washout can remove exudate and hypopyon, but anterior lens-capsule involvement requires caution to avoid capsule injury and cataract. The accompanying table summarizes studies in deep keratomycosis; most reported high success with few complications. Investigators proposed that higher concentrations in deep corneal layers reduce infiltration and resolve endothelial plaques. Most used Amphotericin B 5–10 µg in 0.1 mL; some used Voriconazole 50–100 µg in 0.1 mL. Inadequate response can lead to repeat injection up to 13 times. Reported complications include transiently increased hypopyon and intraocular pressure, postoperative pain, and intrastromal bleeding. In a single randomized controlled trial, Sharma et al found no difference from topical treatment in healing time or final visual acuity, but reported more cataracts after intracameral injection.

document_sections.heading: Rose Bengal Photo-Dynamic Antimicrobial Therapy (PDAT)
document_sections.content: Bascom Palmer Eye Institute initiated in vitro investigation of PDAT using rose bengal as a photosensitizer. Its Ocular Biophysics Laboratory reported activity against Fusarium Solani, Aspergillus fumigatus, Candida albicans, and other fungi. Subsequent clinical efficacy was reported in Fusarium Keratoplasticum keratitis resistant to multiple antifungals. Treatment used rose bengal 0.1% followed by green light delivering 2.7 J/cm2; the patient underwent two rose Bengal PDAT sessions. Infection was successfully treated without reported complications or recurrence within 10 months. The authors consequently describe in vivo safety and report no resistance.

document_sections.heading: Photo-Activated Chromophore for Keratitis-Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking (PACK-CXL)
document_sections.content: UV photoactivation of riboflavin releases reactive oxygen species and promotes covalent bonding between collagen fibers. Reported corneal effects of CXL include increased biomechanical stiffness, collagen-fiber diameter, resistance to enzymatic breakdown, and shrinking temperature, together with reduced swelling. Studies reported biomechanical stability equivalent to standard treatment with higher-intensity CXL at 30 mW/cm2 for 3 min; within a power range of 45–90 mW/cm2, stability did not differ statistically significantly from corresponding lower-intensity treatment. Iseli et al first described clinical CXL for infective keratitis in 2008, treating five microbial-keratitis cases successfully. Although its antimicrobial mechanism was then unknown, they used it because UV has antimicrobial effects and increased corneal tensile strength might limit deep microbial invasion. The PACK-CXL term was proposed at the 9th International Cross-Linking Congress in Dublin in 2013 to distinguish infectious-keratitis treatment from cross-linking for corneal ectasia; it can refer to any chromophore activated to stiffen the cornea. Described modifications to the Dresden protocol include manually removing epithelium from the ulcer surface and margins, debriding discharge and necrotic tissue to improve riboflavin penetration, and potentially using the removed material for microbiology. Riboflavin is used without a viscosity agent, the UV beam is aimed at the lesion even near the limbus, and fluorescein should be avoided because competition for UVA absorption reduces efficacy. PACK-CXL was reported ineffective against viral and acanthamoeba keratitis and has been reported to reactivate herpes simplex virus. Price et al described dendritic lesions after PACK-CXL for a culture-negative melting cornea; CXL is therefore better avoided with active herpetic keratitis or a history of recurrent herpetic keratitis. Clinical studies have reported variable efficacy. PACK-CXL has been proposed alone or with antimicrobials for bacterial or fungal disease and for mixed infection, which poses greater risks of failure and complications. In vitro, in vivo, and clinical studies have reported antimicrobial benefit, particularly in moderate ulcers, with faster healing and epithelialization and fewer perforations; other studies found no added benefit over standard antimicrobials. Most used the Dresden protocol. Tabibian et al first used an accelerated protocol, UVA irradiation at 365 μm and 9 mW/cm2 for 10 min, reporting less infiltration and faster healing. Hafezi et al later used UVA 9 mW/cm2 for either 10 min, 13 min, or 20 s, with fluence of either 5.4 J/cm2 or 7.2 J/cm2. Awad et al tested fluence up to 15 J/cm2 in rabbit eyes and reported better clinical, microbiological, and pathological outcomes. Hafezi et al also reported significant clinical improvement after repeated high-fluence PACK-CXL. The accompanying table summarizes studies of CXL in fungal keratitis. Despite extensive study, PACK-CXL still requires adjustments to UV fluence (J/cm2), irradiation duration, and riboflavin concentration to achieve 100% microbial killing.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: Antifungal treatment is recommended once a smear or positive culture confirms the clinical diagnosis. Intrastromal antifungal injection may sustain therapeutic corneal concentrations. Intracameral injection may be effective for severe disease with deep stromal infiltration that does not respond to treatment. Collagen cross-linking (CXL) has been proposed either as a standalone treatment or as an adjunct to antifungal drugs.
